items_missed: No greeting of any kind. The call opens 'How can I help you?' — no company name, no rep name. The customer had to ask for someone else by name ('Hey, is Cal available?'), Frank answered 'I can see if he's available. Who's calling?' and then took the call himself without ever saying who he was. Six minutes later the customer signs off with 'Alright, brother' still not knowing the name of the person who just scheduled and priced a service day for him.

Never asked 'how are you today?' and no agenda statement or 'sound good?' — he went straight from identifying the account to 'Okay, and you wanted to switch the date you said,' which was also a wrong assumption about why the customer called.

Moving stressors never asked, and the customer stated one plainly at the end: 'we're kind of at the point where we're like run out of room and better house as we living it. So we're like just easier to do something just with the move associates.' That is the actual reason he is buying packing services and it drew no acknowledgment at all.

No hourly rate was ever stated. He priced the pack day entirely in totals — '$740 for that portion' and 'it'd be $575 plus, you know, if we use materials' — both of which resolve to $230/hr for a two-mover team if you do the arithmetic, which the customer has no way to do on the phone. This is an existing customer who already knows the rate from his move quote, which makes it forgivable but not correct: the rate is what lets him judge whether three hours is the right number to buy.
What's-included list entirely absent. Nothing about gas, truck, taxes, insurance, pads, wrap, bands or tools.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. The customer is adding a day where Einstein crews handle every fragile item in his kitchen and two closets — the exact scenario the coverage exists for — and it never came up.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned, and this call set a brand-new arrival window from scratch: 'I have you down for between 12:00 and two that we can get started.' That is the moment for it.

No 'no hidden fees' pitch, and a $50 materials line was added without any framing: 'I'm just gonna put $50 in an estimated cost materials, in case you don't have enough stuff, but it's just for numbers.'

Clock start and fifteen-minute proration both never mentioned. The minimum was implied through its price ('If it takes less than that, obviously it's just the minimum. So it'd be $575') but never named as two and a half hours, and the customer was never told the clock starts on site or that time bills in quarter-hour increments — which is the entire mechanism that protects him if the pack runs short.
No typical pack-time range for a partial pack of this scope, and no crew size stated. The customer does not know if two people or four are showing up between noon and two.
No equivalents or plain-language anchors used to make three hours feel like the right amount of time for roughly fifteen to twenty boxes.

Consolidation examples and the 'take a carload' tip never came, even though the prep-saves-money idea did. He got the principle out — 'obviously the more you do before we get there still they'll just keep costs down' — and then gave the customer nothing actionable to do with it, on a call that was explicitly about the customer running out of time and space.

Email handoff never offered. The customer had to ask for it himself, as an afterthought: 'yeah, if you want to re email me that quote that's fine.' Frank's entire response was 'Correct, yup,' which is a confirmation of the time window in the same sentence, not an explicit commitment to send anything. There is no confirmation that an email is coming, no bolded-details framing, and no 'reply with any corrections' verification ask on a change that moved a scheduled job.

No deposit, business hours, how-to-reach-us, and 'any other questions before I let you go?' all absent. The customer opened this call trying to reach a specific person and ended it with no name and no direct number for the person who actually served him.
Customer's name never used once. He gave it in his second sentence — 'Nate, how we have a quote and a move scheduled in October' — and it was never spoken again.
top_strength: Frank's best quality on this call is that he solved the customer's problem faster than the customer could explain it, and he solved it in the right order. The customer called with a half-formed request — he had packed some of the house, run out of time, and wanted to know what it would cost to hand the rest over — and Frank immediately got him to a room-by-room scope with one question: 'I see. Let's see what do you think is left? Like just kitchen items, closets?' That produced a real inventory (six kitchen boxes, ten across two closets, five across two offices) in about fifteen seconds. He then answered the pricing-model question cleanly and immediately volunteered the money-saving version without being asked: 'Charge by the hour. And then we charge for each packing material that we use. If you have your own boxes, we can use users but we'll bring stuff to.' When the customer asked whether his own Home Depot boxes were acceptable, Frank did not hedge — 'Yeah, totally fine. It'll save on the cost, yeah.' That is a rep actively lowering his own ticket because it is the right answer. The scheduling instinct was the strongest on this board: he identified the sequencing problem himself, before the customer raised it, and proposed the fix in one move — 'we'll have to do that the day before the move, if that's okay cause it looks like you're already, you're okay, good. Okay, so then, we can shoot for Saturday October 10th, probably pack in the afternoon and then we move you on the eleventh as originally planned.' He then actually booked it live with a specific window ('between 12:00 and two'), confirmed the existing move day was untouched ('the eleventh is on, is the same I didn't touch that'), and read the window back when the customer repeated it. No other rep on this board closed a new commitment that cleanly. He also got the core Save Your Ass idea across in his own words and tagged it with a check-in the customer answered: 'obviously the more you do before we get there still they'll just keep costs down you know what I mean?' — 'No, that's perfect.'
coaching_note: Fit caveat first, so the score is read correctly: this is an add-on call to an already-booked customer, not a fresh sales call. Home size, stairs, access, trip fee, disassembly and several estimate variables were all scoped on the original booking, so the N/A rule grants those points and the probe and estimate sections score higher than the conversation itself would suggest. The three sections that genuinely measure this call are Set Agenda (3/7), Pricing (8/20) and Quote/Booking (3/11), and all three are weak. Highest-leverage fix, and it is not subtle: Frank never said his name or the company's. 'How can I help you?' is how you answer your own cell phone, not an inbound line for a customer whose job is on the schedule. The customer called asking for Cal, got Frank instead, was served well, and hung up unable to tell anyone who helped him — which means the next call comes in asking for Cal again. Every call opens with 'Einstein Moving, this is Frank' and closes with 'my name's Frank, here's the direct number.' Estimate-accuracy flag for the bottom-4 review — this is the clearest padding-by-agreement instance in the batch. The customer described his own remaining scope as 'probably only gonna be maybe fifteen twentieth most boxes left if that probably less than that honestly' and then explicitly invited padding: 'I would overestimate just, just to be safe.' Frank's answer was 'Just to be safe, yeah, okay, let me see... Yeah, I could probably just, you know, call like a three hour day and just see where we fall.' Buying the padding because the customer offered it is still padding, and it is the exact managers-run-conservative pattern the estimate-accuracy work is chasing. The correct move keeps the customer's comfort and the accuracy both: 'Fifteen to twenty boxes across a kitchen, two closets and two offices is honestly a two to two-and-a-half hour job for a two-man crew, which is our minimum anyway at $575. I'll book the window wide so we are not rushing you, but I'm not going to quote you three hours for work I think takes two — you only pay for the time we use, in fifteen-minute increments.' That answers 'to be safe' with the proration mechanism instead of with a padded number, and it costs nothing. Worth pulling the actual against this one on October 10th. Second priority: he never committed to sending anything. The customer asked for the quote by email almost apologetically and got 'Correct, yup' in response to a compound sentence. On a call that changed a scheduled job — added a service day, added a crew, added roughly $740 — there has to be a written confirmation with the details called out and a 'reply if anything there is wrong.' Right now the only record of this change lives in Frank's head and whatever he typed into the system. Third: the Save Your Ass speech was half-delivered and worth completing. He got the principle out but gave no examples, and this customer is the ideal recipient — he is packing alongside Einstein, he is out of room, and he told you so. 'Between now and the tenth, anything loose you can throw in a box yourself — the stuff in drawers, closet floors, whatever's in the offices that isn't paper — comes straight off the pack clock. Even a couple of carloads to the new place helps. Does that make sense?'
phone_presence_notes: Easy, accommodating and clearly trusted — the customer ends on 'you guys have been awesome, thank you so much' and 'Alright, brother' — but nearly all of the warmth in this exchange is coming from the customer's side: Frank never greeted him, never used his name, never acknowledged the out-of-room-and-out-of-time comment, and his own contributions are short and functional ('Okay, okay,' 'Just to be safe, yeah, okay, let me see').
audio_review_reason: The clarity deduction rests on evidence that could easily be line quality rather than rep delivery. He failed to catch the email address on the first pass — 'I'm sorry. Can you spell that down? I did not pick up it anywhere you said' — and the transcript is heavily broken through the pricing section ('kitchens can take longer than perspectively looking at, it just depends'). Audio would separate a bad connection from a rep who was talking through his own screen work, and would also confirm whether the customer's repeated 'That's fine. That's fine.' was agreement or resignation.
